claim: Root gravitropic bending represents a fundamental aspect of terrestrial plant physiology.
source: Root gravitropic bending represents a fundamental aspect of terrestrial plant physiology.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about plant physiology.

claim: Gravity is perceived by sedimentation of starch-rich plastids (statoliths) to the bottom of the central root cap cells.
source: Gravity is perceived by sedimentation of starch-rich plastids (statoliths) to the bottom of the central root cap cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gravity perception in plants.

claim: Following gravity perception, intercellular auxin transport is redirected downwards leading to an asymmetric auxin accumulation at the lower root side.
source: Following gravity perception, intercellular auxin transport is redirected downwards leading to an asymmetric auxin accumulation at the lower root side causing inhibition of cell expansion, ultimately resulting in downwards bending.
evidence: This is established knowledge about gravitropic response mechanisms.

claim: Asymmetric auxin accumulation at the lower root side causes inhibition of cell expansion, ultimately resulting in downwards bending.
source: Following gravity perception, intercellular auxin transport is redirected downwards leading to an asymmetric auxin accumulation at the lower root side causing inhibition of cell expansion, ultimately resulting in downwards bending.
evidence: This is established knowledge about how auxin asymmetry leads to gravitropic bending.

claim: How gravity-induced statoliths repositioning is translated into asymmetric auxin distribution remains unclear.
source: How gravity-induced statoliths repositioning is translated into asymmetric auxin distribution remains unclear despite PIN auxin efflux carriers and the Negative Gravitropic Response of roots (NGR) proteins polarize along statolith sedimentation, thus providing a plausible mechanism for auxin flow redirection.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: PIN auxin efflux carriers polarize along statolith sedimentation.
source: How gravity-induced statoliths repositioning is translated into asymmetric auxin distribution remains unclear despite PIN auxin efflux carriers and the Negative Gravitropic Response of roots (NGR) proteins polarize along statolith sedimentation, thus providing a plausible mechanism for auxin flow redirection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PIN protein behavior during gravitropism.

claim: Negative Gravitropic Response of roots (NGR) proteins polarize along statolith sedimentation.
source: How gravity-induced statoliths repositioning is translated into asymmetric auxin distribution remains unclear despite PIN auxin efflux carriers and the Negative Gravitropic Response of roots (NGR) proteins polarize along statolith sedimentation, thus providing a plausible mechanism for auxin flow redirection.
evidence: This is established knowledge about NGR protein behavior during gravitropism.

claim: NGR1-GFP localizes to the statolith periphery.
source: NGR1-GFP displayed a highly specific columella expression, which was most prominent at the PM and the statolith periphery.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: NGR1-GFP is significantly polarized to the bottom area of columella cells.
source: NGR1-GFP signal from the PM was not evenly distributed, but rather polarized to the lower side of the columella cells in the vicinity of the sedimented statoliths (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations and quantification shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NGR1-GFP polarization occurs in the vicinity of sedimented statoliths.
source: NGR1-GFP signal from the PM was not evenly distributed, but rather polarized to the lower side of the columella cells in the vicinity of the sedimented statoliths (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 1A.

claim: NGR1p::NGR1-GFP fully rescued the agravitropic bending phenotype of the ngr1/2/3 triple mutant.
source: This construct fully rescued the agravitropic bending phenotype of the ngr1/2/3 triple mutant (see further), proving functionality of the GFP-tagged protein.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on gravitropic bending assays.

claim: NGR1-GFP construct is functional.
source: This construct fully rescued the agravitropic bending phenotype of the ngr1/2/3 triple mutant (see further), proving functionality of the GFP-tagged protein.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue of the mutant phenotype.

claim: 35Sp::NGR1-GFP localizes to the plasma membrane in multiple cell types.
source: Constitutive overexpression of NGR1-GFP under 35 S promoter (35Sp::NGR1-GFP) confirmed that in multiple other cell types, NGR1-GFP localizes to the PM suggesting direct membrane binding mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations of overexpression lines.

claim: NGR1 localizes to chloroplasts in guard cells.
source: Additionally, NGR1 is associated with other plastid types such as chloroplasts in guard cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: NGR1-GFP localizes at the chloroplast periphery.
source: To separate the GFP signal from the chlorophyll, we used fluorescence lifetime imaging, which confirmed that NGR1-GFP localizes at the chloroplast periphery (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence lifetime imaging data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Chloroplasts in the vicinity of the PM correlate with NGR1 accumulating at the PM nearby.
source: Notably, chloroplasts in the vicinity of the PM strongly correlated with NGR1 accumulating at the PM nearby, similar to the scenario in columella (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and C.

claim: NGR1-GFP relocalizes dynamically with falling statoliths following gravitropic stimulus.
source: Following gravitropic stimulus, NGR1 at the PM relocalized dynamically with the falling statoliths (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: NGR1 signal at the top membrane decreases after gravitropic stimulation.
source: First, the signal at the top membrane decreased and then reached the bottom PM together with statoliths, around 5 min after the stimulation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: NGR1 signal reaches the bottom PM together with statoliths around 5 min after gravitropic stimulation.
source: First, the signal at the top membrane decreased and then reached the bottom PM together with statoliths, around 5 min after the stimulation (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and D.

claim: When roots are rotated 180° from vertical position, it takes more than 15 min for statoliths to fall.
source: If the root was rotated 180° from the vertical position (from root tip pointing down to pointing up), the time required for the statolith sedimentation has increased due to the cell's elongated shape and the presence of vacuole. In such a scenario, it took more than 15 min for the statoliths to fall.
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy observations.

claim: The increase of NGR1 signal at the bottom side correlates with statolith occurrence.
source: Again, the increase of the NGR1 signal at the bottom side correlated with the statolith occurrence, implying that statolith vicinity is the region where NGR1 signal gets enriched (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NGR1 signal always decorates the PM proximal to the statolith when monitored for an extended period.
source: When monitored for an extended period of time, NGR1 signal was always decorating the PM proximal to the statolith (Video 1).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse video microscopy shown in Video 1.

claim: Calcium transients at the bottom side of the root are visible within a minute after statoliths touch the bottom membrane.
source: While the signal increase at the bottom side of the root was visible within a minute after statoliths touched the bottom membrane, its decrease at the top PM started immediately after rotation.
evidence: This is supported by GCaMP calcium sensor data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Calcium signal decrease at the top PM starts immediately after rotation.
source: While the signal increase at the bottom side of the root was visible within a minute after statoliths touched the bottom membrane, its decrease at the top PM started immediately after rotation.
evidence: This is supported by GCaMP calcium sensor data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The first signaling event in root gravitropic bending is the statolith removal from the top membrane, rather than its arrival at the bottom.
source: This implies that the first signaling event in the root gravitropic bending is the statolith removal from the top membrane, rather than its arrival at the bottom (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of calcium transient changes shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The first visible PIN3 polarization to the bottom columella cell sides is detectable only after 15 minutes.
source: While subsequent changes in the DII-Venus degradation were consistent with the calcium-based timing, the first visible PIN3 polarization to the bottom columella cell sides was detectable only after 15 minutes (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data of PIN3-GFP shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The earliest auxin asymmetry is generated by PIN-mediated polar auxin transport.
source: Nonetheless, already the earliest auxin asymmetry is likely generated by PIN-mediated polar auxin transport as it was completely blocked by the treatment with N-1-naphthylphthalamic acid (NPA) (Figure 1E), a PIN inhibitor (Abas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by NPA treatment experiments shown in Figure 1E and cited literature.

claim: NPA is a PIN inhibitor.
source: Nonetheless, already the earliest auxin asymmetry is likely generated by PIN-mediated polar auxin transport as it was completely blocked by the treatment with N-1-naphthylphthalamic acid (NPA) (Figure 1E), a PIN inhibitor (Abas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Abas et al., 2021.

claim: NPA treatment completely blocks the earliest auxin asymmetry.
source: Nonetheless, already the earliest auxin asymmetry is likely generated by PIN-mediated polar auxin transport as it was completely blocked by the treatment with N-1-naphthylphthalamic acid (NPA) (Figure 1E), a PIN inhibitor (Abas et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by NPA treatment experiments shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Statolith sedimentation is accompanied by rapid NGR1 relocation to the PM subdomain proximal to the NGR1-containing statoliths.
source: To summarize, statolith sedimentation is accompanied by rapid NGR1 relocation to the PM subdomain proximal to the NGR1-containing statoliths.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The first event in gravitropic response is NGR1 leaving the top membrane accompanied by decrease in auxin signaling at the upper root side.
source: The first event in gravitropic response is the NGR1 leaving the top membrane accompanied by decrease in the auxin signaling at the upper root side, followed by NGR1 arrival at the bottom membrane and increase in auxin signaling at the bottom side.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: NGR1 arrival at the bottom membrane is followed by increase in auxin signaling at the bottom side.
source: The first event in gravitropic response is the NGR1 leaving the top membrane accompanied by decrease in the auxin signaling at the upper root side, followed by NGR1 arrival at the bottom membrane and increase in auxin signaling at the bottom side.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: Initial auxin asymmetry is mediated by PIN-dependent auxin transport despite visible polarization of PIN3 being detected only later.
source: This initial auxin asymmetry is mediated by PIN-dependent auxin transport, despite visible polarization of PIN3 can be detected only later.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: RLD trafficking is sensitive to the ARF-GEF inhibitor Brefeldin A (BFA).
source: As RLD trafficking is known to be sensitive to the ARF-GEF inhibitor Brefeldin A (BFA) (Furutani et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2022), we examined if the drug also affects the localization and polarization of NGR1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Furutani et al., 2020 and Wang et al., 2022.

claim: NGR1-GFP does not accumulate into BFA compartments.
source: Interestingly, while FM4-64-stained membranes accumulated into so-called BFA compartments, NGR1-GFP did not and still showed association with the PM and amyloplasts (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by BFA treatment experiments shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: NGR1-GFP still shows association with the PM and amyloplasts after BFA treatment.
source: Interestingly, while FM4-64-stained membranes accumulated into so-called BFA compartments, NGR1-GFP did not and still showed association with the PM and amyloplasts (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by BFA treatment experiments shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The polarization of NGR1 following gravity stimulation is not disrupted in the presence of BFA.
source: Furthermore, the polarization of NGR1 following gravity stimulation was not disrupted in the presence of BFA.
evidence: This is supported by BFA treatment experiments.

claim: Overexpressed NGR1 does not show co-localization with BFA aggregates.
source: Similar effects were observed in overexpressed NGR1 as it also did not show co-localization with BFA aggregates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by BFA treatment experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: NGR1 localization and gravity-induced polarization does not undergo BFA-sensitive endocytic recycling mediated by the ARF-GEF GNOM.
source: This shows that NGR1 localization and gravity-induced polarization does not undergo BFA-sensitive endocytic recycling mediated by the ARF-GEF GNOM as it has been shown for other proteins involved in gravity response like RLDs and PINs (Geldner et al., 2001; Naramoto et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2022).
evidence: This is inferred from the BFA treatment experiments and supported by citations.

claim: DTT treatment causes NGR1-GFP to show an increase in cytoplasmic signal and reduction of PM association.
source: Following previously described conditions, NGR1-GFP showed an increase in cytoplasmic signal and reduction of PM association (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by DTT treatment experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: NGR1 still localizes to amyloplasts after DTT treatment.
source: Interestingly, NGR1 still localizes to amyloplasts, indicating a different way of plastid association compared to the PM.
evidence: This is supported by DTT treatment experiments.

claim: PAO treatment significantly increases NGR1-GFP cytosolic signal.
source: NGR1p::NGR1-GFP seedlings were incubated for 30 min with 30  µM phenylarsine oxide (PAO), a PtdIns(4)-kinase inhibitor (Hammond et al., 2012; Vermeer et al., 2009). The NGR1-GFP cytosolic signal was significantly increased, indicating that the interplay between PBRs and phospholipids is important for NGR1 PM but not amyloplast association (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by PAO treatment experiments shown in Figure 2D and cited literature.

claim: PAO is a PtdIns(4)-kinase inhibitor.
source: NGR1p::NGR1-GFP seedlings were incubated for 30 min with 30  µM phenylarsine oxide (PAO), a PtdIns(4)-kinase inhibitor (Hammond et al., 2012; Vermeer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hammond et al., 2012 and Vermeer et al., 2009.

claim: The interplay between PBRs and phospholipids is important for NGR1 PM but not amyloplast association.
source: The NGR1-GFP cytosolic signal was significantly increased, indicating that the interplay between PBRs and phospholipids is important for NGR1 PM but not amyloplast association (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from PAO treatment experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: FEN treatment causes NGR1-GFP to show an increase in cytoplasmic signal and membrane localization is largely lost.
source: NGR1-GFP seedlings were grown on fenpropimorph (FEN), an inhibitor of sterol biosynthesis that decreases the number of sterols and can trigger their conversion into cyclopropyl sterols (Frescatada-Rosa et al., 2014). NGR1-GFP showed an increase in cytoplasmic signal and membrane localization was largely lost (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by FEN treatment experiments shown in Figure 2D and cited literature.

claim: FEN is an inhibitor of sterol biosynthesis that decreases the number of sterols and can trigger their conversion into cyclopropyl sterols.
source: NGR1-GFP seedlings were grown on fenpropimorph (FEN), an inhibitor of sterol biosynthesis that decreases the number of sterols and can trigger their conversion into cyclopropyl sterols (Frescatada-Rosa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Frescatada-Rosa et al., 2014.

claim: LOV treatment has comparable effects to FEN treatment on NGR1-GFP localization.
source: Comparable effects were also observed after treatment with another sterol synthesis inhibitor lovastatin (LOV) (Figure 2D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by LOV treatment experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: DTT, PAO, FEN, and LOV treatments do not disturb NGR1 amyloplast localization.
source: However, similarly to DTT and PAO, amyloplast localization could not be disturbed.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological treatment experiments.

claim: NGR1 PM localization depends on acylation, phospholipid, and sterol membrane composition.
source: These observations show that NGR1 PM but not necessarily plastid localization depends likely on acylation, phospholipid, and sterol membrane composition.
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological treatment experiments.

claim: NGR1 has two polybasic regions: K113K114R115K116 (PBR1) and K186K187K188R189 (PBR2).
source: We noticed 2 PBRs K113K114R115K116 (PBR1) and K186K187K188R189 (PBR2) – these strands of positively charged amino acids may mediate the interaction of NGR1 with negatively charged phospholipids.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis of NGR1.

claim: NGR1 has a conserved Cys206 residue that is a potential S-palmitoylation site.
source: Also, we noticed a conserved Cys206 residue – a potential S-palmitoylation (PALM) site according to the GPS-Lipid post-translational modification prediction tool (Xie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis and prediction tool, supported by citation.

claim: NGR1-PALM-GFP restored the anti-gravitropic root phenotype of the ngr1/2/3 triple mutant similar to NGR1WT-GFP.
source: The NGR1-PALM version resembled the root bending of the NGR1WT-GFP version, and NGR1-PBR2 and NGR1-PBR1&2 versions demonstrated a slight delay in the main root angle restoration after reorientation in the vertical scanner setup (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by gravitropic bending assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: NGR1-PBR2 and NGR1-PBR1&2 versions demonstrated a slight delay in the main root angle restoration after reorientation.
source: The NGR1-PALM version resembled the root bending of the NGR1WT-GFP version, and NGR1-PBR2 and NGR1-PBR1&2 versions demonstrated a slight delay in the main root angle restoration after reorientation in the vertical scanner setup (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by gravitropic bending assays shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The PM/cytoplasm ratio was slightly decreased for NGR1-PALM-GFP, NGR1-PBR2-GFP, and NGR1-PBR1&2-GFP mutants compared to NGR1WT-GFP.
source: The PM/cytoplasm ratio was slightly decreased for NGR1-PALM-GFP, NGR1-PBR2-GFP, and NGR1-PBR1&2-GFP mutants compared to NGR1WT-GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: NGR1p::NGR1-PALM&PBR2-GFP could not fully complement ngr1/2/3 triple mutant.
source: NGR1p::NGR1-PALM&PBR2-GFP and NGR1p::NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2-GFP could not fully complement ngr1/2/3 triple mutant.
evidence: This is supported by gravitropic bending assays.

claim: NGR1p::NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2-GFP could not fully complement ngr1/2/3 triple mutant.
source: NGR1p::NGR1-PALM&PBR2-GFP and NGR1p::NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2-GFP could not fully complement ngr1/2/3 triple mutant.
evidence: This is supported by gravitropic bending assays.

claim: The main root of 5 d.o. seedlings expressing NGR1-PALM&PBR2 or NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 demonstrated inclination from the vertical angle.
source: The main root of the 5 d.o. seedlings demonstrated inclination from the vertical angle (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by phenotypic observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: NGR1-PALM&PBR2 displayed partially compromised restoration of the main root angle upon reorientation.
source: In contrast to NGR1-GFP complemented ngr1/2/3 plants, complementation with NGR1-PALM&PBR2 displayed partially compromised restoration of the main root angle upon reorientation, while the NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 root bending was completely disrupted (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by gravitropic bending assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 root bending was completely disrupted.
source: In contrast to NGR1-GFP complemented ngr1/2/3 plants, complementation with NGR1-PALM&PBR2 displayed partially compromised restoration of the main root angle upon reorientation, while the NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 root bending was completely disrupted (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by gravitropic bending assays shown in Figure 3B.

claim: NGR1-PALM&PBR2 and NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 dissociate from the PM.
source: With confocal microscopy we observed the dissociation of the NGR1-PALM&PBR2 and NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 from the PM (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3C.

claim: PM/cytoplasm ratio was significantly decreased for both NGR1-PALM&PBR2 and NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 compared to non-mutated NGR1-GFP.
source: PM/cytoplasm ratio was significantly decreased for both NGR1-PALM&PBR2 and NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 compared to non-mutated NGR1-GFP (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The combination of mutations in PBRs and palmitoylation site results in the decrease of NGR1-GFP PM binding and loss of the protein functionality.
source: Taken together, the combination of mutations in PBRs and palmitoylation site resulted in the decrease of NGR1-GFP PM binding and loss of the protein functionality.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: The N-terminus of LZY1 mediates its membrane localization potentially via a predicted N-myristoylation site.
source: It was shown that the N-terminus of LZY1 mediates its membrane localization potentially via a predicted N-myristoylation site (Yoshihara and Spalding, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yoshihara and Spalding, 2020.

claim: The LZY1 N-terminal myristoylation site is not conserved in NGR1.
source: This site is not conserved in the NGR1.
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: LZY1 does not possess the palmitoylated Cys residue conserved in NGR1.
source: Remarkably, LZY1 does not possess the palmitoylated Cys residue conserved in NGR1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: NGR1Nmyr -PALM&PBR1&2 membrane association was partially restored.
source: NGR1Nmyr -PALM&PBR1&2 membrane association was partially restored, and NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 ROP-CT membrane association was fully restored (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations and quantification shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 ROP-CT membrane association was fully restored.
source: NGR1Nmyr -PALM&PBR1&2 membrane association was partially restored, and NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 ROP-CT membrane association was fully restored (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations and quantification shown in Figure 3E and F.

claim: The gravitropic response of NGR1Nmyr -PALM&PBR1&2-GFP and NGR1-PALM&PBR1&2 ROP-CT-GFP plants was restored.
source: In accordance with PM localization, the gravitropic response of those plants was also restored (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: This is supported by gravitropic bending assays shown in Figure 3G and H.

claim: NGR1 PM localization is mediated synergistically by PBRs and palmitoylation site.
source: Thus NGR1 PM localization is mediated synergistically by PBRs and palmitoylation site, and the NGR1 PM association is crucial for NGR1 functioning in root gravitropic response.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: NGR1 PM association is crucial for NGR1 functioning in root gravitropic response.
source: Thus NGR1 PM localization is mediated synergistically by PBRs and palmitoylation site, and the NGR1 PM association is crucial for NGR1 functioning in root gravitropic response.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: D6PK is a well-established PIN3 activating kinase.
source: To test this, we analyzed the localization of D6PK, a well-established PIN3 activating kinase (Willige et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Willige et al., 2013.

claim: YFP-D6PK and mCH-D6PK display translocation to the new bottom side of columella cells following 180° rotation.
source: Following 180° rotation, YFP-D6PK and mCH-D6PK displayed a very clear translocation to the new bottom side of the columella cells (Figure 4A–C).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: D6PK polarization following gravistimulation is absent in ngr1/2/3 triple mutants.
source: Notably, following gravistimulation, D6PK polarization was absent in ngr1/2/3 triple mutants (Figure 4C–D, Video 2).
evidence: This is supported by time-lapse microscopy data shown in Figure 4C-D and Video 2.

claim: Other cell types such as meristematic cells or epidermal cells display undisturbed basal D6PK polarity in ngr1/2/3 triple mutant.
source: Surprisingly, other cell types such as meristematic cells or epidermal cells still displayed undisturbed basal (WT-like) D6PK polarity in ngr1/2/3 triple mutant suggesting a role of NGRs in D6PK targeting specifically during gravity response (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NGRs play a role in D6PK targeting specifically during gravity response.
source: Surprisingly, other cell types such as meristematic cells or epidermal cells still displayed undisturbed basal (WT-like) D6PK polarity in ngr1/2/3 triple mutant suggesting a role of NGRs in D6PK targeting specifically during gravity response (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that D6PK polarity is affected only in columella cells of ngr1/2/3 mutants.

claim: D6PK, a PIN activating kinase, is translocated towards the bottom columella cell sides in an NGR-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, we identified D6PK, a PIN activating kinase to be translocated towards the bottom columella cell sides in an NGR-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented.

claim: NGR-dependent D6PK translocation provides a plausible mechanism for rapidly redirecting auxin fluxes prior to PIN relocation during root gravitropic response.
source: This provides a plausible mechanism for rapidly redirecting auxin fluxes prior to PIN relocation during root gravitropic response.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: The temporal correlation between NGR1 relocation and auxin asymmetry dynamics was tested by monitoring auxin-dependent calcium transients.
source: The temporal correlation between NGR1 relocation and auxin asymmetry dynamics was tested by monitoring auxin-dependent calcium transients.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used.

claim: A decline in calcium transients occurs at the upper root side preceding the auxin-induced calcium wave at the bottom side.
source: Interestingly, while an auxin-induced calcium wave can be observed following statolith descent to the bottom side of the gravity-sensing cells, preceding this, a decline in calcium transients occurs at the upper root side.
evidence: This is based on calcium imaging data.

claim: The first signaling event in root gravitropic bending may be the departure of statoliths from the upper PM, not statolith contact with the cell bottom.
source: These observations suggest that the first signaling event in root gravitropic bending may not be statolith contact with the cell bottom, but rather the departure of statoliths from the upper PM, closely followed by NGR1 and D6PK translocation to the bottom cell sides.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the timing of calcium transients.

claim: The departure of statoliths from the upper PM is closely followed by NGR1 and D6PK translocation to the bottom cell sides.
source: These observations suggest that the first signaling event in root gravitropic bending may not be statolith contact with the cell bottom, but rather the departure of statoliths from the upper PM, closely followed by NGR1 and D6PK translocation to the bottom cell sides.
evidence: This is based on the timing of observed events.

claim: PIN auxin exporters polarize significantly later than NGR1 and D6PK.
source: Only significantly later, similar polarization of PIN auxin exporters can be confidently observed.
evidence: This is based on the timing of observed events.

claim: Some degree of root bending was observed already within the first 5 min following gravistimulation.
source: This may be reflected by actual onset of the root bending, as there is growing evidence, that the actual root bending begins much sooner than previously reported, in fact, some degree of bending was observed already within the first 5 min following gravistimulation (Dubey et al., 2023; Serre et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dubey et al., 2023 and Serre et al., 2023.

claim: NGR-GFP relocation to the new bottom membrane happens rapidly and is not affected when ARF GEF-mediated endomembrane trafficking is inhibited.
source: NGR-GFP relocation to the new bottom membrane happens rapidly and is not affected when ARF GEF-mediated endomembrane trafficking is inhibited.
evidence: This is based on BFA treatment experiments.

claim: The NGR1 membrane anchoring mechanism is dependent on cysteine acylation and adjacent polybasic stretches.
source: The NGR1 membrane anchoring mechanism is dependent on cysteine acylation and adjacent polybasic stretches, which interact with charged lipids at the membrane surface.
evidence: This is based on mutagenesis and pharmacological experiments.

claim: Polybasic stretches of NGR1 interact with charged lipids at the membrane surface.
source: The NGR1 membrane anchoring mechanism is dependent on cysteine acylation and adjacent polybasic stretches, which interact with charged lipids at the membrane surface.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data on membrane composition effects.

claim: The mechanism of NGR1 membrane targeting is rather universal.
source: Since we could restore the protein functionality by adding two different membrane anchors on the NGR1 N and C terminus, we conclude that the mechanism of membrane targeting is rather universal.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with different membrane anchors.

claim: Point mutated NGR1 proteins which lost their membrane binding ability still retained the statolith binding.
source: Point mutated NGR1 proteins which lost their membrane binding ability still retained the statolith binding, implying an independent targeting mechanism.
evidence: This is based on microscopy observations of mutant proteins.

claim: NGR1 has independent targeting mechanisms for PM and statolith association.
source: Point mutated NGR1 proteins which lost their membrane binding ability still retained the statolith binding, implying an independent targeting mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PM and statolith binding can be separated.

claim: Statolith-bound NGR1 is not sufficient for the NGR1 function in gravitropism.

claim: PIN polarization has been shown to be reliant on NGR proteins.

claim: PIN polarization occurs too late to account for the initial auxin asymmetry.

claim: Gravity-induced polarization of D6PK AGCVIII kinases is contingent on NGR activity.

evidence: This is based on the experimental data showing D6PK polarization is absent in ngr mutants.

claim: Prior to relocation of PIN transporters, AGCVIII-mediated PIN activation at the lower cell sides rapidly redirects auxin fluxes following gravity perception.

claim: The model plant Arabidopsis thaliana senses gravity in central root cap (columella) cells and the shoot endodermal cells.

claim: Gravity-sensing cells contain starch-enriched plastids called amyloplasts.

claim: Due to their higher density, amyloplasts act as statoliths and sediment within cells.

claim: Following amyloplast sedimentation, PIN3 and PIN7 polarize towards the bottom cell sides.
source: Following amyloplast sedimentation, the PIN exporters for the plant hormone auxin (PIN3 and PIN7) polarize towards the bottom cell sides, thus creating a downwards polarized auxin flow, which correlates with the asymmetric auxin accumulation at the lower side of the organ mediating the shoot/root curvature (Friml et al., 2002; Kleine-Vehn et al., 2010; Rakusová et al., 2011; Band et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.
